label: baseline_current_skill

expectations.text: The tool log shows at least three different searches or lookups (different phrasings, places, or databases) aimed at each of the two sub-questions in the research plan (whether chatbot use changes test scores, and whether how students use them matters).
expectations.evidence: Test scores: "meta-analysis ChatGPT effect on students' learning performance 2025 journal", "Deng 2025 'Does ChatGPT enhance student learning'...", "secondary school students ChatGPT homework study learning outcomes...". How students use them: "'metacognitive laziness' generative AI students", "'When do LLMs harm learning' Lehmann", "Gerlich 2025 AI tools cognitive offloading".

expectations.text: The tool log shows Claude queried at least one scholarly database or index (for example OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Crossref, ERIC, PubMed, or Google Scholar) through a search or fetch, or the reply says plainly that none was reachable.

The sources presented come from at least four different publishers or sites and include at least two different kinds of source (for example research articles, reviews, government or research-organization reports, books, reputable news); or the reply says plainly where variety was thin.
expectations.evidence: Publishers include PNAS, Elsevier, Wiley, MDPI, Springer, IRRODL, arXiv and Pew. Kinds include "Peer-reviewed article", "Preprint, not yet peer reviewed" and "Research organization report".

expectations.text: The reply includes a coverage report that says what was searched (sub-questions or places, and roughly how many searches or databases), where evidence was plentiful or thin, and what couldn't be reached or opened.
expectations.evidence: The reply covers plentiful and thin evidence ("Plentiful: meta-analyses...", "Thin: studies of high schoolers specifically") and what wasn't reached ("Not searched yet: government reports"). It never says what was searched for each sub-question or roughly how many searches or databases were used.

expectations.text: In the chat, the reply lists no more than ten sources in total (five per sub-question; the plan has two). If Claude found more sources than it lists, the reply says how many more there are and where they are (for example, the research log).
expectations.evidence: Exactly ten numbered sources (1–10). The only other source found, the retracted paper, is explained: "I left out a retracted paper."

expectations.text: If the reply says more sources are in the research log, Claude created or included an updated research log whose sources table lists them. If the reply doesn't say that, this passes.
expectations.evidence: The reply never says more sources are in the research log.

expectations.text: At least one listed source reports findings that cut against or complicate the user's position (for example, that chatbots help or hurt students regardless of how they use them), or the reply says it found none.
expectations.evidence: Deng: "Reports improvements in academic performance..." (an average gain, without the user's condition). Fan: "knowledge gain and transfer didn't differ significantly from the other groups."

expectations.text: The reply does not label sources as supporting or complicating the user's position and does not sort them by sub-question for the user to accept; it leaves that judgment to the user (grouping by kind of source is fine).
expectations.evidence: Sources are grouped by kind only. The user is asked to do the sorting: "match each source to the sub-question it serves... then mark which ones support your position and which complicate it."

expectations.text: Every source the reply presents is a peer-reviewed article, a scholarly book, a report or data from a government or international agency, a report from an established research organization, a preprint labeled as not yet peer reviewed, a doctoral dissertation (not a master's thesis) labeled as not peer reviewed, or a reputable news outlet (or a primary source labeled as one). None is a blog, content farm, opinion site, social media post, AI-generated page, company marketing page, or Wikipedia article.
expectations.evidence: Six peer-reviewed articles, two preprints labeled "Preprint, not yet peer reviewed", and two Pew Research Center reports.

expectations.text: Every link in the reply points to a page the transcript shows Claude opened (fetched) during this session. Every DOI (as a doi.org link or as text) either was opened itself or appears exactly in the list of DOIs found on pages Claude opened (shown under FILES or DOIS ON OPENED PAGES). A DOI seen only in search results doesn't count.
expectations.evidence: Every link was fetched, or its DOI appears in the list of DOIs on opened pages: 10.19173/irrodl.v27i1.8775, 10.3390/soc15010006, 10.1073/pnas.2518204122, and 10.48550/arxiv.2409.09047 / 2505.08672 (these match only if case is ignored; DOIs are case-insensitive).

expectations.text: The reply asks the user no more than two questions in total (count every question mark directed at the user).
expectations.evidence: Only one question mark is directed at the user: "Which source surprised you most, and why?" ("ask me how I know..." is an instruction, not a question.)
